fr:mainmatter.html:p: This library is not about formalizing category theory as an end in itself.

html:div.html:p: The category theory we implement is a means to support formalized metatheory. It just happens that category theory provides the right abstractions.

html:blockquote.html:p: Litmus test. Enough theory to support compositional semantic constructions for simple typed lambda calculi.

html:div.html:p: When we implement, we work backwards from this goal.

fr:title.text: Encoding category theory in intensional type theory

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Encoding category theory in intensional type theory

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Our setting forces nonstandard design choices.

html:div.html:p: We are immediately led to displayed categories as a fundamental construction — well-suited to a non-evil encoding of category theory in intensional type theory.

html:blockquote.html:p: A category is to a context as a displayed category is to a dependent type.

html:ul.html:li: Extends the cubical standard library, occasionally upstreaming results
Heavy use of function extensionality
Light on univalence, though ongoing experiments may change this
Effectively --safe: only a couple of guarded-calculi files break this

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Metatheoretic proofs often follow a common structure:

html:ul.html:li: Construct a semantic model encoding the desired property
Interpret the syntax of the language in the model
Profit

html:div.html:p: Choice of language and semantic domain vary across applications, but the overall architecture of a proof is static.
Despite this, formalized developments are often ad-hoc and lack reuse.

html:blockquote.html:p: Category theory provides a natural framework for reuse across applications.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A simple logical relation.

html:div.html:p: Define a predicate \llbracket {A}\rrbracket _{\mathrm {Canonical}} on closed terms for each type A, then show that all closed terms inhabit the predicate.
Concretely, for booleans:
Other logical relations take the same shape: proofs living over syntactic terms.

html:blockquote.html:p: How can we categorify this observation?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Where do the typing derivations live?

html:div.html:p: The syntactic category \mathsf {Syn} for a simple language of products and functions over a signature \Sigma :

html:ul.html:li: Objects: types (or contexts)
Morphisms: A \to B are well-typed terms x : A \vdash t : B, modulo \beta \eta .

html:div.html:p: \mathsf {Syn} is a Cartesian closed category, and moreover it is the free Cartesian closed category over \Sigma .

html:ul.html:li: For any CCC \mathcal {C} equipped with an interpretation \iota : \Sigma \to \mathcal {C}, there is a unique CCC-functor \mathsf {Syn} \to \mathcal {C} extending \iota .

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A canonical form depends on a term.
The fundamental theorem is then a dependent function (M : \mathsf {Term}~A) \to \mathsf {isCanonical}\,M.

html:div.html:p: Terms aren't just a type — they are morphisms in \mathsf {Syn}. So \mathsf {isCanonical} shouldn't be a dependent type; it should be some kind of dependent category.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A category varying over another category.
A displayed category \overline {\mathcal {C}} over \mathcal {C}:

html:ul.html:li: for c : \mathcal {C}, a type \overline {\mathcal {C}}_{c} of displayed objects over c
for f : c \to c' and \overline {c} \in \overline {\mathcal {C}}_{c}, \overline {c'} \in \overline {\mathcal {C}}_{c'}, a type of displayed morphisms over f
and identity, composition, etc.

html:div.style: color: var(--fg-muted); font-style: italic; border-top: 1px dashed var(--rule); border-bottom: 1px dashed var(--rule); padding: 0.4em 0; margin: 0.6em 0

html:div.html:p: A section s : \mathcal {C} \to \overline {\mathcal {C}} picks a displayed object for each base object and a displayed morphism for each base morphism.
A canonicity proof = a displayed category over \mathsf {Syn} + a section.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Constructing a section via universal property.
\mathsf {Syn} is the free Cartesian closed category on \Sigma . Its universal property is a dependent eliminator:

html:div.style: color: var(--fg-muted); font-style: italic; border-top: 1px dashed var(--rule); border-bottom: 1px dashed var(--rule); padding: 0.4em 0; margin: 0.6em 0

html:div.html:p: Universal properties on the syntax specify the action of the eliminator on each term constructor.
To prove canonicity, it suffices to:

html:ul.html:li: Make precise what we mean by a displayed CCC
Construct a displayed CCC to carry the canonical forms

fr:mainmatter.html:p: First, what is a universal property?

html:div.style: color: var(--fg-muted); font-style: italic; border-top: 1px dashed var(--rule); border-bottom: 1px dashed var(--rule); padding: 0.4em 0; margin: 0.6em 0

fr:mainmatter.html:p: By the Yoneda Lemma, a presheaf P : {\mathcal {C}}^{\mathrm {op}} \to \mathrm {Set}, object c \in \mathcal {C}, and element x \in P\,c determine a natural transformation \mathcal {C}[-,c] \Rightarrow P, f \mapsto (P f) x.
We say that x \in P\,x is a universal element if this is a natural isomorphism.

html:blockquote.html:p: Lesson N. Universal elements are a homogeneous interface for universal properties — one record, instantiated for terminals, products, exponentials, etc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Universal properties in a displayed category.

html:div.html:p: A first attempt arises naturally from universal elements:

html:blockquote.html:p: A displayed universal property is a universal element in the total category \int \overline {\mathcal {C}} that lies strictly over the corresponding universal element in the base.

html:div.html:p: This isn't favorable for formalization, as you cannot ask for the index of a dependent type to definitionally live over something after the fact.
Instead, we describe a similar Yoneda-type statement as for ordinary categories.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let P : {\mathcal {C}}^{\mathrm {op}} \to \mathrm {Set} and \overline {\mathcal {C}} a displayed category over \mathcal {C}.
A displayed presheaf^{1} is a presheaf on the category \int _{\mathcal {C}} \left ( \overline {\mathcal {C}} \times \mathsf {Element}(P) \right ).

html:ul.html:li: Locally small category theory — level-polymorphic universal properties via categorical structures displayed over a category of levels

Convenient bifunctor encodings — naive bifunctors aren't definitionally well-behaved when acting by the identity in one component and a nontrivial morphism in the other; we experiment with alternatives that bridge this gap
Logical relations for guarded type theories, including an implementation of guarded canonicity
Compositional metatheory for effectful languages and call-by-push-value
Preliminary 2-categorical concepts — bicategories, double categories, etc.
